"Depose" has two distinct meanings — one from the world of politics and power, and one from the world of law. Both are important, and both are in active use today.
Meaning 1: To Remove a Powerful Leader from Their Position

This is the most common, everyday meaning of "depose."

To depose someone means to forcefully or officially remove a ruler, monarch, or leader from their position of power — usually against that person's will. The key ideas packed into this word are: the person held a very high position (like a king, queen, president, emperor, or dictator), and they were removed — stripped of their authority — typically by force, a rebellion, a coup, or a collective decision by those around them.

The army deposed the king and declared a republic.
The prime minister was deposed after a vote of no confidence.
Rebels deposed the dictator after years of civil unrest.

What makes "depose" different from similar words?

This is important, because several words seem similar but mean different things:

  • Fired / dismissed — These apply to ordinary jobs. You fire an employee. You do not "depose" a school principal or a store manager. "Depose" is reserved for figures of very high authority — heads of state, monarchs, rulers.
  • Resigned — When someone resigns, they choose to leave. Deposing is the opposite — the person is removed by others, often against their wishes. A king doesn't choose to be deposed; it happens to him.
  • Impeached — This one trips people up. To impeach a leader (in systems like the US) means to formally charge them with wrongdoing — like an indictment in court. It's a legal accusation, not a removal. A leader can be impeached and still stay in power. To depose, on the other hand, means the removal has actually happened. Think of it this way: impeachment is the process; deposing is the result of being actually thrown out.

The emotional weight of the word

"Depose" carries a sense of drama, significance, and often upheaval. It suggests that someone who seemed untouchable — someone with immense power — was brought down. This is why you'll see the word frequently in history books, news about political crises, and stories about revolutions or coups. It's a heavy, consequential word.
Meaning 2: To Take Someone's Sworn Testimony (Legal Context)

This meaning lives entirely in the world of law, and it's very specific.

In legal proceedings, to depose someone means to formally question them under oath, outside of a courtroom, usually before a trial begins. A lawyer (or attorney) deposes a witness or involved party by sitting them down, asking them detailed questions, and having every word officially recorded.

The attorney deposed the key witness last Tuesday.
She was deposed for three hours by the defense lawyers.
Before the trial, both sides deposed several company executives.

The formal record that comes out of this process is called a deposition. It is a legally sworn statement — meaning the person being questioned is under oath, just as they would be in court, and lying during a deposition is a serious crime (perjury).

Why does this happen before a trial?

In many legal systems (especially in the US), both sides of a legal case go through a phase called discovery, where they gather evidence and information before the trial starts. Deposing witnesses is a key part of this. It allows lawyers to:

  • Find out exactly what a witness knows and will say
  • Lock a witness into their story (if they say something different later in court, the deposition can be used against them)
  • Build or challenge the case before stepping into a courtroom

Who gets deposed?

Anyone relevant to the case — witnesses, experts, the people being sued, employees of a company involved in a lawsuit, doctors in a medical case, and so on.
The Two Meanings Side by Side

Even though these two meanings sound quite different, here's a way to see the thread connecting them: both involve someone being formally "brought down" or "put in a lowered position." In the political sense, a ruler is brought down from power. In the legal sense, a witness is brought down to a formal, controlled setting and made to answer questions under oath.

• Deposed (adjective/past tense) — "the deposed king lived in exile" / "the witness was deposed yesterday"
  • Deposing (present participle) — "the rebels were planning on deposing the ruler"
  • Deposition (noun) — refers both to the act of removing a ruler ("the deposition of the emperor") and to the legal testimony document ("the lawyer reviewed the deposition")
  • Deponent (noun) — the person who gives testimony in a legal deposition

Political meaningTo forcefully remove a ruler or high-ranking leader from power
Legal meaningTo formally question someone under oath before a trial

In everyday life, if you see "depose" in a history article or news story about a political crisis, it almost certainly means a leader was removed from power. If you see it in a legal context — a courtroom drama, a news article about a lawsuit, or a legal document — it means someone was formally questioned under oath.

That's the full picture of "depose." Two meanings, each sharp and specific, and now entirely yours.
